description: We are the Computer Coolers. We’re an ambitious team of five competing to win. We build fast, make decisions quickly and ship polished work. Our strengths are product-building experience, React and front-end development, and AI-assisted development that takes us from concept to working prototype quickly. We know how to scope a project, cut what doesn’t matter and deliver a demo that’s ready before the deadline. Our team is full, but we’re here to compete seriously and bring our best work.
summary:
NASA satellites have recorded fires for over two decades, but the record comes from two instruments. MODIS has watched since 2000. VIIRS joined in 2012 with pixels seven times smaller. Joined naively, the record shows fire activity jumping three- to five-fold when VIIRS takes over. That is a sharper camera, not more fire. As MODIS retires, every new month risks being judged against the wrong past.
Spark1 repairs that seam. From the years both satellites flew together, we learnt an exchange rate for each region, season and time of day, which rises with fire size because MODIS sees large fires best. The result is one monthly fire calendar since 2002 for mainland Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and California, with an uncertainty band on every month. Tested on years it had never seen, it explained 98% of the variation in what MODIS recorded.
We are five students led by our captain, Aziz. Two data analysts chose the regions and periods and built the record, one teammate shaped it for its users, and two app developers brought it to life. Spark1 offers historical context, not warnings.
details:
MODIS, VIIRS and a 3.3–5.4× jump that isn’t real

If you want to know whether this summer’s fires are unusual, you compare them with past summers. NASA’s satellite fire record lets you do that back to 2002, but there’s a catch: it comes from two instruments that see fires very differently. Aqua MODIS, flying since 2002, has 1 km pixels. VIIRS, on Suomi NPP since 2012 and NOAA-20 since 2018, has 375 m pixels, so it picks up much smaller fires and reports several times more of them. Stitch the raw counts together and fire activity seems to jump 3.3 to 5.4 times, when the only thing that changed was the satellite. And because Aqua’s orbit has been drifting since 2021, the older instrument can’t carry the record on its own anymore.

Spark1: a 24-year burning calendar on a 3D globe

Spark1 is a free web app that puts the whole record on one scale, from July 2002 to 13 November 2026, for four fire-prone regions: mainland Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and California. You open the link (no account needed), pick a region on the globe, draw your own shape or type in coordinates, and choose the months you care about. You get a calendar of every month since 2002, coloured by fire activity, and a plain-language verdict on how the latest month compares with 2003 to 2025, with its uncertainty right next to it. If the month isn’t over yet, it’s compared with the same days in earlier years, so a half-finished November doesn’t look quiet just because it’s half-finished.

A Sensors panel shows the false jump and how our correction removes it. An optional layer puts every raw detection back on the globe, each one sized like its real pixel, so you can see the difference between MODIS and VIIRS with your own eyes. Everything can be downloaded as a CSV, down to each individual hotspot with its time, satellite, confidence, fire power and source.

From raw FIRMS hotspots to 5 km fire cell-days

We removed everything in the NASA FIRMS data that isn’t a new vegetation fire: duplicates, volcanoes like Etna and Stromboli, industrial heat sources, offshore detections, low-confidence points, and repeat sightings of the same fire. About 1.6 million detections remain. Instead of counting raw points, we count “fire cell-days”: a 5 km square counts once on any day it has a fire. That way, a fire VIIRS sees as a dozen small pixels isn’t counted a dozen times.

Converting VIIRS to the Aqua MODIS scale, with 90% ranges

We keep the measured Aqua MODIS record up to June 2021 and convert VIIRS to the Aqua scale after that. The conversion isn’t one fixed ratio. It changes with the region, the season, day or night, and the size of the fires, because a fire has to give off about seven times more heat before MODIS notices it. Every converted month gets a 90% range, and the app always shows it.

Leave-one-year-out validation

We tested it by hiding one year at a time and predicting it from the others. The typical monthly error dropped from 1.55 with raw counts to 0.33 after correction, and 89% of the true values landed inside our 90% ranges. Where the record switches satellite, there’s no longer a significant step.

Seasonal context for land managers, researchers and planners

Land managers planning a season. Researchers asking whether a trend is real or just a change of sensor. Emergency planners, journalists, and people who live in these places. Spark1 is for context, not for decisions during a fire, and it says so, pointing to the NASA FIRMS Fire Map and local authorities for what’s happening right now. It also looks ahead: MODIS won’t fly forever, and the record already carries on with VIIRS alone. The method isn’t tied to these four regions either.

Harmonized record and native pixels on one globe

Spark1 lets you see the corrected record and the raw detections behind it on the same globe. We also worked hard to keep the interface honest. Ranges are always visible. A month with missing satellite days gets “no verdict” instead of a misleading one. Counts are never presented as burned area. One example we like: Sardinia’s July 2021, the month of the Montiferru fire, ranks only 8th of 25 Julys, because our measure counts how widely fires spread across a region, not how intense a single fire was. The app explains that instead of hiding it.

Honest limits, accessibility and reproducibility

A hotspot is a hot pixel, not a confirmed fire, and zero detections doesn’t mean nothing burned: cloud and smoke hide fires. Near-real-time data is provisional, and we label it that way. The year being judged is always left out of its own baseline. We wanted everyone to be able to use it, so it works with a keyboard and a screen reader, offers colour-blind-safe palettes, and fits on a phone. It’s a static site with no accounts and no API keys in the browser. The code is open, and we checked the cleaning rules with a second, independent implementation. Every dataset and library is credited with its licence, and our use of AI is documented in the repository.

Python pipeline, TypeScript app, NASA FIRMS and GIBS data

The data pipeline is written in Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, Shapely, PyArrow), with DuckDB and PostgreSQL for checks. The statistical model uses Poisson means with negative-binomial ranges. The app is TypeScript and React, with MapLibre GL for the globe, Terra Draw for drawing and Observable Plot for the charts, hosted as a static site on Vercel. We test it with Vitest, Playwright and axe: 290 unit tests and 85 end-to-end tests. No special hardware; it runs in any modern browser. NASA data: FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 on Aqua, VIIRS 375 m on Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) and GIBS imagery. Claude helped us write code and documentation.
